title: Deep Learning
premise: Backpropagation built by hand, then the training dynamics that decide whether a network learns anything at all. The gap this closes is specific: you can already call a model and measure it, and you cannot yet look at a loss curve that has gone flat and say why. Everything here is aimed at that — an autodiff engine you wrote, activation statistics you have plotted, and three broken training runs you produced on purpose so the fourth one, which breaks by accident, is recognisable.
why_here: Tenth overall, after the mathematics that makes the chain rule mechanical and the classical grounding that makes the evaluation honest, and immediately before transformers — which is unreadable as anything but magic until you have written the backward pass yourself.
laboratory: A laptop, deliberately. Every network in this course trains on CPU in minutes: a scalar autodiff engine, an MLP on a few thousand examples, a small convolutional net. Nothing here needs a rented GPU, because a course gated on hardware is a course that gets abandoned in week three. The constraint is also the lesson — with no compute to hide behind, a bad initialisation shows up as a dead network rather than as a slightly worse number.
sitting_rule: Every item is completable in one sitting. Nothing exceeds 180 minutes, and anything over 90 declares its own checkpoints.
honesty_note: No advanced standing. Calling PyTorch is not evidence of understanding autodiff, and the portfolio contains no trained network, no gradient statistics and no ablation.

panel.blind_note: Judges see the submission and the rubric, never each other's scores, and never the learner's self-assessment.
panel.disagreement: Scores are reported per judge and never averaged into a single number when the spread is 2 or more on any criterion.
panel.bias_warning: Judges are instructed that a small network trained on a laptop is the intended scale, and that a submission must not be marked down for using a toy dataset where the rubric asks about mechanism rather than performance.

items.title: Your own autodiff engine
checkpoints: Forward pass with a graph that records its own operations
Backward pass implemented with topological ordering
Gradients matched against torch.autograd on the same expression
One non-trivial function — a division or a power — added and checked
items.brief: Write a scalar reverse-mode autodiff engine: a value type that records the operations performed on it, and a backward pass that walks the graph in topological order accumulating gradients. Do not consult micrograd's source while writing it; consult it afterwards and note the differences. Verify against torch.autograd on an expression with at least one repeated variable, because that is where naive implementations silently overwrite instead of accumulating.

items.title: Train something with the engine you wrote
checkpoints: An MLP assembled from your own value type
A training loop with a stated loss and optimiser
Loss decreasing on a real task
The same task trained in PyTorch for comparison
items.brief: Build a small multi-layer perceptron out of your own engine and train it on something real enough to have a wrong answer — a two-class problem from your own data, or a standard small dataset. Get the loss down. Then train the same architecture in PyTorch and compare both the final loss and the wall-clock time. The gap in speed is the point at which you understand what a framework is actually buying you.

items.title: How autograd works in the framework
items.locator: The tensors tutorial and the autograd mechanics tutorial — the dynamic graph, leaf tensors, and when gradients are freed.

items.title: Where your engine and the framework part company
checkpoints: At least three concrete differences identified
Each stated as a design trade rather than a defect
One demonstrated with code
items.brief: Name at least three things PyTorch does that your engine does not — graph freeing, in-place operation tracking, broadcasting, vectorisation, higher-order gradients. For each, say what it buys and what it costs, and demonstrate one of them with a snippet where your engine would give the wrong answer or run out of memory. This is a comparison, not an apology: a scalar engine is not trying to be a framework.

items.title: Instrument a training run
checkpoints: Activation statistics recorded per layer per epoch
Gradient norms recorded per layer
Update-to-weight ratio computed
A healthy run characterised numerically, not visually
items.brief: Take a network that trains successfully and instrument it: activation means and standard deviations per layer, gradient norms per layer, and the ratio of update magnitude to weight magnitude. Record all of it across training. Then write down what healthy looks like as numbers — the ranges you observed — because a diagnostic you can only apply by squinting at a plot is one you will not apply at 2am.

items.title: Three broken runs, and the tell for each
checkpoints: Three distinct failures produced from one base run
The instrumentation from M2.3 applied to each
The earliest distinguishing signal identified for each
A diagnostic procedure written and then tested blind
items.brief: Break the same training run three ways — a dead network from bad initialisation, a diverging one from too high a learning rate, and one that trains but does not generalise. Apply your instrumentation to each and find the earliest point at which they are distinguishable from one another and from the healthy run. Then have someone, or a script, hand you the four runs unlabelled and see whether your procedure identifies them. Report your accuracy at that, including if it is poor.

items.title: Initialisation decides whether it learns
checkpoints: Three initialisation schemes implemented
Activation variance measured layer by layer at step zero
Training outcome recorded for each
The measured variance related to the scheme's derivation
items.brief: Initialise the same deep network three ways — all zeros, a naive Gaussian with fixed scale, and a fan-in-aware scheme such as He or Xavier. Before training, measure the activation variance at every layer and show it growing or collapsing with depth. Then train all three and report what happened. Finish by connecting the measurement to the derivation: the scheme exists to keep that variance constant, and your numbers either show that or they do not.

items.title: Does normalisation help here, or is it cargo
checkpoints: A baseline without normalisation, tuned
Normalisation added and re-tuned rather than dropped in
Both compared across multiple seeds
The effect on learning rate sensitivity measured separately from final accuracy
items.brief: Add batch or layer normalisation to a network you have trained, and find out whether it actually helps on your problem. Tune the learning rate separately for each version, because normalisation's main effect is often on how tolerant the network is of the learning rate rather than on final accuracy — and comparing at a single shared rate hides that entirely. Run several seeds. Report both effects separately, and be willing to conclude it made no difference.

items.title: Implement an architecture from its diagram alone
checkpoints: Architecture chosen and its diagram cited
Implemented without consulting a reference implementation
Parameter count computed by hand and checked against the model
Reference implementation consulted afterwards and differences listed
items.brief: Pick an architecture with a published diagram — a small ResNet block, an LSTM cell, or an encoder block — and implement it from the diagram and the paper's text alone. Do not open a reference implementation until you have finished. Compute the parameter count by hand from the shapes and check it against what the framework reports; a mismatch means you misread the diagram, and finding out where is the assignment. Then open the reference and list what you got wrong.

items.locator: The chapters on convolutional neural networks and on recurrent neural networks — the implementations alongside the explanations.

items.title: Ablate the component nobody questions
checkpoints: One component removed cleanly
Parameter count held roughly constant, or the difference accounted for
Multiple seeds run
A conclusion stated about whether it earns its place
items.brief: Take the architecture you implemented and remove one component that is normally taken for granted — the skip connection, the gate, the normalisation layer. Keep the parameter count roughly constant so you are testing the component and not the capacity. Run several seeds and report whether it earned its place on your problem at your scale. The honest answer at small scale is frequently that it did not, and saying so is worth more than reproducing the expected result.

modules.title: Scale, and a network of your own

items.title: Scaling laws for neural language models
Training compute-optimal models
items.locator: Read against the previous paper: the interesting content is where the two disagree about how to spend a fixed compute budget, and why.

items.title: A scaling curve you measured yourself
checkpoints: At least four model sizes trained to convergence
Compute accounted for per run
Loss plotted against a compute or parameter axis
The limits of extrapolating from this range stated
items.brief: Train the same architecture at four or more sizes on a laptop, to convergence, and plot final loss against parameter count or against compute. You will get a curve. Then do the part that separates this from a plot: say what it does and does not license. Four small points over one order of magnitude cannot support an extrapolation to a model a thousand times larger, and the papers you just read are the standard of evidence you are being compared against.

items.title: The network you built, and what its curves showed
checkpoints: Written for a reader who has trained nothing
Instrumentation plots included with their ranges explained
At least one negative result included
Published and connected backwards to an earlier chapter
items.brief: Publish a chapter of the public engineering log covering what you built and, more importantly, what the instrumentation showed. Include at least one thing that did not work — the ablation that came out flat, the normalisation that made no difference, the scaling curve that was too short to conclude from. It must connect backwards to an earlier chapter; the autodiff engine and the AIE-201 backpropagation derivation are the obvious links.

items.title: Oral defense
items.brief: Three unscripted questions generated from your own submissions at defense time, answered aloud without notes.
sample_question_shapes: Your engine accumulated gradients for a repeated variable. Walk me through what would have happened if it had assigned instead, and at which point in training you would have noticed.
You concluded batch norm made no difference. A reviewer says you must have tuned it wrong. Answer them.
Your scaling curve has four points. Someone extrapolates it two orders of magnitude in a meeting. What do you say?

rubrics.integrity: Conceding a real error is scored as strength. A defense in which the author never yields is evidence of stubbornness rather than understanding.

completion.required: All eight assignments, the project and the defense submitted. Readings and lectures are tier 0 and are tracked but never counted toward mastery.
completion.grade_rollup: Deterministic. Each item's tier sets its weight; panel scores enter as per-criterion values; nothing is rounded up. Computed in TypeScript, never by a model.
completion.mastery_note: Sets initial mastery on the four deep-learning skills and evidences PyTorch and the numeric stack as a byproduct rather than as objectives. FSRS then decays them.
